Here's what you can follow.

Month 1: Arrays & Strings
→ Arrays: Two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums, subarrays, sorting
→ Strings: Hashing, palindrome, substring search, two pointers

Month 2: Linked Lists & Stacks/Queues
→ Linked Lists: Fast & slow pointers, reversal, merge/intersection
→ Stacks/Queues: Monotonic stack, min/max stack, queue simulation

Month 3: Trees
→ BFS, DFS, recursion, binary search tree, tree diameter, lowest common ancestor

Month 4: Graphs & Heaps
→ Graphs: BFS, DFS, topological sort, shortest path, cycle detection, components
→ Heaps: Min-heap, max-heap, heap applications

Month 5: Intervals & Advanced Patterns
→ Intervals: Merge intervals, sweep line
→ Greedy: Scheduling, activity selection
→ Bit Manipulation, Backtracking basics

Month 6: Dynamic Programming (DP)
→ 1D/2D DP, subsequence/substring, knapsack, state compression, DP on trees

Cracking interviews isn't about solving problems.
It's about showing how you think.

If you're preparing, don't just grind.

You're serious about preparing the right way, get the 1:1 guidance from experts to start- https://bit.ly/4m1TqGc

Practice the way interviews actually happen:
 👉 Clarify before coding.
 👉 Explain while solving.
 👉 Show trade-offs, not just answers.
 👉 Talk impact, not effort.

This is the part most people miss.

I've sat through 100+ interviews, and I can tell you this: rejections rarely happen because someone can't code.

They happen because someone can't communicate their thinking under pressure.

Here's what interviewers are really checking for:

* In DSA rounds, they want to see if you ask the right questions before rushing into code. Can you think in patterns instead of brute force?
* In system design, they don't expect you to architect “the next Google.” They want to see if you can break down complexity, highlight trade-offs, and keep things simple.
* In behavioral rounds, they don't want a list of responsibilities. They want to know the impact you created and how you handled challenges.

And here's the truth about today's market: with AI + automation reshaping engineering, companies want people who can adapt, reason, and explain—not just type code faster.

That's why even brilliant engineers with years of experience are getting filtered out.
So don't just “prepare problems.” Prepare like you're already in the room.

Also, now platforms like Tutort Academy are genuinely helpful (have helped more than 2150+ professionals switch careers in top tech companies). They help you build industry-relevant projects, prep for tech interviews, and stay updated with what's being asked, including GenAI.

Because at the end of the day — interviewers aren't just hiring problem solvers.
They're hiring thinkers.

Is Agentic AI making software engineers slower? 🤔 

A recent study found experienced developers were 19% slower with AI, despite feeling more productive. 

This is because the bottleneck is shifting from writing code to validating it. 

AI is evolving from a “co-pilot” assistant to a proactive “agent” capable of handling complex tasks. 

Our role is shifting from writing every line of code to becoming strategic architects and critical reviewers. 

The future may see human engineers orchestrating teams of specialized AI agents to deliver entire features. 

I think the best skill to develop today is being a generalist who can work with this human-AI partnership. 

With AI, churning out code regularly, critical judgement is the key.
